concerns: The paper presents a comparative study but does not establish its claimed contribution of a first comprehensive comparison: the literature review itself lists ViT and fusion models already applied and evaluated, the models compared are standard baselines rather than new methods, and no independent test-set verification of the headline results is supplied. Multiple stated performance values for nearly identical measures are inconsistent, such as the conclusion reporting TransUNet mIoU 0.64 and Dice 0.54 while Table IV reports 0.67 and 0.52, so the reported claims cannot be treated as scientifically reliable.

The central fairness claim is not supported by the noted optimization signals in Table III: U-Net and TransUNet use Dice loss while ViT uses Cross-Entropy, and batch sizes, maximum epochs, and early-stopping dynamics differ, so the alleged rigorous gold-standard comparison does not establish equivalence of training conditions. Such protocol mismatch can materially distort Dice and mIoU rankings and invalidates the central conclusion of this comparative benchmark.

The headline results are reported from validation curves and best-epoch selection rather than a held-out test assessment. The stated best-performing model was selected using peak validation mIoU, yet no test-split metrics are actually reported, even though the paper earlier declares a test split, meaning the results may have been selected for the very metric being reported.
scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The study offers an empirical benchmarking exercise, but methodological inconsistencies in training setups (differing loss functions, epochs, and batch sizes) prevent a rigorous apples-to-apples architectural comparison. Combined with reporting peak validation scores rather than transparent test split results, scientific certainty is insufficient for promotion.

Three different benchmark databases were used to ensure diversity in the studied materials, defect categories, 
and imaging conditions. 
• MVTec Anomaly Detection (AD) Benchmark [4]: Contains 5,354 high -resolution images categorized 
into 15 object and texture classes, including metals, fabrics, leather, and electronic components with 
defects such as scratches, dents, and cracks.  
• NEU Surface Defect Benchmark: A steel surface inspection dataset containing 1,800 images across 
multiple defect categories including crazing, inclusion, patches, pitted surfaces, rolled -in scale, and 
scratches.  
• DAGM 2007 Benchmark [16]: A texture defect benchmark consisting of 1,150 images covering six 
different defect categories.  
The merged dataset containing 8,304 images was split into training (70%), validation (20%), and testing (10%) 
datasets with balanced distribution across each split.

The U -Net was used as the CNN -based baseline, where the pre -trained ResNet-34 encoder was used with a 
symmetrical decoder, where both were linked via skip connections for each scale level. The encoder down -
samples the input using convolutional layers and max pooling, while the decoder up -samples the image using 
transposed convolution layers combined with skip connections from the encoder to restore spatial information. 
The 1×1 segmentation layer generated the output probability map for binary classification of defects. Since U -
Net performs very well on small amounts of annotated data sets, it is considered a strong competitor.

Transformer (ViT), and TransUNet, in the context of industrial manufacturing applications. The experiments 
were conducted using three datasets with similar settings, which allowed for a reliable architectural comparison 
of the models.

model convergence and accurate boundaries. ViT yields high mean intersection over union (0.72) but shows a 
better generalization pattern with well -aligned training and validation curves and monotonic convergence.

missing_information: No reproducible review or selection methodology was detected.

blocking_reasons: The paper presents a comparative study but does not establish its claimed contribution of a first comprehensive comparison: the literature review itself lists ViT and fusion models already applied and evaluated, the models compared are standard baselines rather than new methods, and no independent test-set verification of the headline results is supplied. Multiple stated performance values for nearly identical measures are inconsistent, such as the conclusion reporting TransUNet mIoU 0.64 and Dice 0.54 while Table IV reports 0.67 and 0.52, so the reported claims cannot be treated as scientifically reliable.

The central fairness claim is not supported by the noted optimization signals in Table III: U-Net and TransUNet use Dice loss while ViT uses Cross-Entropy, and batch sizes, maximum epochs, and early-stopping dynamics differ, so the alleged rigorous gold-standard comparison does not establish equivalence of training conditions. Such protocol mismatch can materially distort Dice and mIoU rankings and invalidates the central conclusion of this comparative benchmark.

The headline results are reported from validation curves and best-epoch selection rather than a held-out test assessment. The stated best-performing model was selected using peak validation mIoU, yet no test-split metrics are actually reported, even though the paper earlier declares a test split, meaning the results may have been selected for the very metric being reported.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The evaluation is based on supervised training against dataset ground-truth masks with validation mIoU and Dice metrics computed as overlap with those human-annotated labels; no model-based judge, reward, or automated evaluator appears to be used to optimize or score outcomes.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Peak validation mIoU and Dice coefficient values across epochs are the headline results, although no distinct test-set metrics are reported.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised optimization with ground-truth masks using BCE and Dice loss for U-Net and TransUNet and Cross-Entropy for ViT under AdamW, with early stopping and learning-rate decay.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding a unified, controlled experimental setup are undermined by the differing hyperparameters and loss functions between architectures in Table III. The claimed trade-offs between generalization and inductive bias are loosely supported given the lack of independent test set quantification.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation relies on selecting peak validation mIoU epochs and reports aggregated performance on the combined dataset without per-dataset or per-class breakdowns. In addition, the paper states that the best checkpoint was chosen to evaluate test results, yet the primary results presented in Table IV and the figures reflect validation epoch metrics rather than a distinct test set evaluation.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Standard supervised training where evaluation is conducted on ground truth pixel annotations rather than a model-based reward or tuning judge.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Validation set mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Dice coefficient metrics computed across epochs.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised loss functions (AdamW with Dice loss for U-Net/TransUNet and Cross-Entropy for ViT) optimized against ground truth masks.

primary.limitations: The authors identify limitations regarding binary classification, computational costs of transformers, and evaluation within a controlled synthetic/benchmark environment rather than real-world manufacturing lines.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology trains standard baseline models on a combined pool of datasets using different training settings (Table III shows unequal epochs, batch sizes, and loss functions across the models, such as Dice Loss vs Cross-Entropy). Furthermore, the exact ViT decoder architecture used for dense pixel segmentation is inadequately described.
primary.quality_rationale: The study offers an empirical benchmarking exercise, but methodological inconsistencies in training setups (differing loss functions, epochs, and batch sizes) prevent a rigorous apples-to-apples architectural comparison. Combined with reporting peak validation scores rather than transparent test split results, scientific certainty is insufficient for promotion.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper presents an empirical comparison of three deep learning segmentation models (U-Net, ViT, and TransUNet) trained on a merged industrial defect dataset comprising MVTec AD, NEU, and DAGM 2007.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The study offers an empirical benchmarking exercise, but methodological inconsistencies in training setups (differing loss functions, epochs, and batch sizes) prevent a rigorous apples-to-apples architectural comparison. Combined with reporting peak validation scores rather than transparent test split results, scientific certainty is insufficient for promotion.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors identify limitations regarding binary classification, computational costs of transformers, and evaluation within a controlled synthetic/benchmark environment rather than real-world manufacturing lines.

limitations_or_uncertainty.value: Structured research-card claims use title, abstract/summary, metadata, screening rules, and curation. A separate scholarly-quality assessment used bounded full-text excerpts, but unsupported claim, method, or evidence fields remain unextracted.

research_relevance.value: Directly relevant to computer-vision research based on screening evidence.
